title: Speak good or stay silent
hookLine: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, speak good or be silent, honor the neighbor and the guest (Nawawi 15, Abu Hurayrah)
carry: say good or stay silent, and honor neighbors
tomorrow: a man asks for advice and gets two words. why say them again?

cards: Saturday, seven in the morning, and the line at a coffee counter runs out the door. The man at the front has waited four minutes and wants everyone to hear about it.

Behind the counter, the answer is already loaded, and it is sharp, and it would feel great. Across the street, the owner of a brand-new bakery is unlocking her door for the first time, glancing over. A customer waiting.
A neighbor watching. One sentence could go either way, and there's a hadith built for exactly this second.

teach.b: Al-Nawawi's fifteenth hadith, in paraphrase. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say good or stay silent.
Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. Look at how it's built: the same opening three times.
Faith in the Last Day, the biggest thing there is, gets checked in three small places.

teach.h: THE MOUTH, THE FENCE, THE DOOR.
teach.b: The mouth. The fence. The front door.
And the first line offers two doors, not one.
Not 'only say nice things.' Not 'never speak.' Good, or silent. If what's coming is good, say it. If it isn't, the second door is always open, and it costs nothing.
Silence here isn't sulking or the cold shoulder; it's simply not adding the bad sentence. Then the neighbor. The hadith doesn't ask what the neighbor believes.

teach.h: HAVE YOU SENT SOME NEXT DOOR?
teach.b: One report has the Prophet's companion Abdullah ibn Umar, when a sheep was slaughtered at his house, asking twice: have you sent some to our Jewish neighbor?
Then he quoted the Prophet: Jibril kept urging me about the neighbor until I thought he'd make him an heir.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the sheep, the question asked twice, and the neighbor of another faith at the center of it.

how: This hadith is memorized as part of al-Nawawi's Forty and quoted at home, in class and in Friday sermons; in some homes it shows up as a plate sent next door and tea for whoever drops by.

o: khayr: what's worth saying out loud
khayr: polite words, true or not

games.q: the mouth, the fence, the door — tap the pairs.
p: whoever's on the other side of the wall
asked twice about the Jewish neighbor

s: the hadith says the safest thing is to stay quiet
it gives two doors: say good, or be silent. good speech comes first.
the same opening, belief in Allah and the Last Day, comes three times
faith gets checked at the mouth, the neighbor and the guest.
in the tradition, 'neighbor' means a Muslim neighbor only
Ibn Umar asked twice whether meat had gone to his Jewish neighbor, and quoted the Prophet on neighbors.

games.q: your group chat is roasting a classmate who isn't in it. you have a genuinely funny line ready. by today's hadith, what's the move?
o: post something good about her, or post nothing.
post it with 'jk'; a joke isn't really speech.
leave every chat that ever has gossip in it.
games.why: good, or silent: two doors. a joke at someone's expense isn't the first one, and the second door is always open.

practice: Close your eyes and let the day's first complaint come up: a slow line, a late reply, the noise next door. Don't say it, not even in your head.
Hold it like a cup you've decided not to pour, and let it cool for the length of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Good: khayr in Arabic, the first door in today's hadith. If it's good, say it. If it isn't, the second door, silence, never locks.

orig.note: Arabic: good, goodness. In the hadith, 'let him say khayr, or stay silent.'

carryVoice: Your line: say good or stay silent, and honor neighbors. The neighbor on the other side of the wall counts too. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 15; Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, Sahih Muslim 47 (Abu Hurayrah)
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1943; Sunan Abu Dawud 5152 (Ibn Umar and the Jewish neighbor; Jibril kept urging about the neighbor)
